historical_evidence.finding: Within-game did_adapt toward SHOULD counters improves PPP, but the apparent adapter advantage (+0.05–0.07 PPP) was produced by selection and regression-to-the-mean artifacts, not a genuine counter lift.

Play-type classifier assisted-flag leak: SPOT_UP 2.83 PPP (100% makes) because the assisted flag existed only on made shots. After rewrite, SPOT_UP ~1.16 PPP. Shows that outcome-derived labels can catastrophically inflate play-type efficiency.

Turnover-force matchup decomposition on four playoff games: player-channel n often 15–28 defensive possessions; primary defender attribution includes helper steals. Failure: exposure sparsity makes reliable lift estimation impossible.
On-ball defensive scheme labeling: only 14.9% and 3.3% of possessions labeled in two teams; 'switches_on' field unpopulated. Label error and small sample prevented any usable scheme-lift analysis.
Within-series DID-ADAPT case study (NYK vs PHI): n=8 team-game rows; series SHOULD vector missing; adaptation effects untestable due to small sample.

Holdout play-type rank validation: median rank correlation +0.539, but top-3 lift partly reflects league-wide high-efficiency play types (CUT, PUTBACK, TRANSITION); 10.5% of rows misleading (rho<0). Highlights that apparent counter lift can be an artefact of play-type base rates.

failed_approaches.why: Selection and regression-to-the-mean artefacts; adapter dPPP advantage vanished after controlling for early PPP quintiles; SWITCH subgroup reversed.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Possession-level play-type PPP from original PBP classifier
failed_approaches.why: Assisted-flag leakage (flag present only on makes) produced absurd PPP values (SPOT_UP 2.83). Demonstrates how easily outcome-dependent labelling contaminates efficiency measures.
Exposure sparsity: player-channel n often 15–28, too small for reliable PPP estimation; primary_defender attribution includes helper steals, further blurring the channel.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Labelling on-ball defensive schemes from NBA matchup/PBP fields
failed_approaches.why: Label rates 3–15%; 'switches_on' unpopulated; classification error and small sample made scheme-based analysis untestable.
Sample size n=8 team-game rows; missing SHOULD vector prevented computation; small sample made adaptation effects untestable.

evidence_establishes: Conditional lift analyses that condition on a failure event are highly vulnerable to regression-to-the-mean (SF13).
Play-type PPP measures derived from play-by-play can be contaminated by outcome-derived flags, producing catastrophic overestimates (SF-PAP-096).
Rare play sequences yield very small cell sizes, making reliable PPP estimates impossible at the level of individual teams or matchups (SF-APPA-066, SF-APPA-004).
Even play-type ranking models show that top-performing play types often simply reflect league-wide high-efficiency play types rather than genuine counter effects (SF-APPA-063).
Defensive scheme labels from standard NBA data feeds are too sparse and error-prone to condition a counter analysis (SF-APPS-058).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether PULL_UP after a PNR failure yields positive lift.
The magnitude or prevalence of any such lift across NBA teams or seasons.
That the 'PNR fail → PULL_UP' sequence occurs frequently enough to support a league-wide test.
That any observed lift would be causal rather than an artefact of selection, base rates, or data leakage.
own_inferences: The study would require defining 'PNR fail' precisely (e.g., turnover, missed shot, defensive stop with zero points) and identifying the next possession's play type as PULL_UP. The combined filter will produce very small sample sizes per team-season, likely far below what is needed to estimate PPP lift with adequate power.

The threshold of '>=70% of units with median lift>2pp' implies a per-unit significance test; with ~30 teams, even if the effect is real, sampling variation and multiple testing will make the criterion very difficult to meet without large samples.
The absence of a pre-specified counterfactual baseline (lift relative to what?) makes the hypothesis ill-posed; inadvertent choice of baseline could create or mask an effect.

Even if a positive lift were observed, it would be indistinguishable from regression to the mean following a failure event, or from the generally high efficiency of certain shot types (like PULL_UP) relative to league average.
uncertainties: Exact definition of 'PNR fail' not given by the research question; what counts as a failure (e.g., any non-score, only turnovers, shot clock violations) is ambiguous.
Baseline PPP for computing 'lift' is unspecified: league-average PULL_UP PPP, team-average PULL_UP PPP, or PPP after non-failure PNRs?
The unit of analysis ('units') is not stated; typical candidates are team-season or team-series, each with different power implications.
The number of possessions meeting the PNR-fail-then-PULL_UP sequence has not been estimated; without a pilot count, sample size is unknown but likely small.
Temporal constraints: 2025-26 season is partial; using full dataset may still yield sparse sequences.

historical_effect.explanation: Without historical evidence, one might optimistically attempt a simple PPP comparison. The prior work shows that conditional lift after a failure (SF13) was an RTM artefact, play-type PPP can be wildly distorted by outcome leaks (SF-PAP-096), and rare-event sample sizes prevent reliable estimation (SF-APPA-066, SF-APPA-004). These findings collectively demonstrate that a naive test of this hypothesis is almost certain to produce a misleading result, shifting the decision from potential proceed to do_not_proceed.

blocking_constraints.text: PNR-fail-then-PULL_UP sequences are rare per team-season; expected counts likely too low to estimate per-unit PPP lift with sufficient precision for the 70% / 2pp thresholds.
Even league-wide, the number of such sequences may be sparse, making median lift estimates unstable and power for per-unit tests very low.
Conditioning on a PNR failure selects low-PPP possessions; subsequent PULL_UP efficiency will regress upward even if pull-up is not a counter, creating a spurious lift.

prior_work.summary: No prior study tested the exact hypothesis that PULL_UP after PNR failure is a league-wide counter. However, earlier work on adaptation lift after defensive failures (SF13) was found to be an RTM artefact; play-type efficiency measures were contaminated by look-ahead leaks (SF-PAP-096); and rare-event decomposition suffered from extreme exposure sparsity (SF-APPA-066). These findings are directly applicable to the proposed analysis and strongly caution against a simple PPP-comparison test.

risks.text: Conditioning on PNR failure selects possessions with low outcomes; any subsequent play type will appear to have higher PPP due to regression to the mean, even without a counter effect.
Play-type classification uses assisted flags that may exist only for made shots; if unaddressed, pull-up PPP could be inflated by makes that were assisted, mimicking a lift.
Identifying PNR and PULL_UP from PBP data relies on accurate play-type inference; classification errors (as seen in SF-PAP-096, SF-APPS-058) can bias PPP estimates.
PNR-fail-then-PULL_UP sequence is expected to be rare; per-unit sample sizes likely too small for reliable lift estimation (analogous to SF-APPA-066).
Even if the effect exists, the test demands that >=70% of units show positive lift with median >2pp; with few sequences per unit, power to detect such an effect is extremely low.
PULL_UP jumpers after a PNR failure may systematically differ in shot quality (defender proximity, shot clock, score differential) from pull-ups in other contexts, confounding the lift estimate.
Testing positive lift across many units inflates false positive risk; without appropriate multiplicity correction, the 70%-of-units threshold may be trivially met by chance.
If PNR failure is defined using the outcome of the possession (e.g., missed shot), the definition itself conditions on the very outcome we later analyse, creating circularity.

design.estimand: The causal effect on points per possession (PPP) of a team executing a PULL_UP jump shot on the possession immediately following a pick-and-roll (PNR) that ended without points (turnover, missed field goal, non-shooting foul, or shot-clock reset), relative to that team's pull-up PPP in comparable game states that do not follow a failed PNR, adjusting for shot quality and context.
design.unit: Team-season (up to 120 units across four seasons, though 2025-26 is partial at time of query)
design.sample: All NBA possessions from 2022-23 through 2025-26 (complete regular season plus playoffs) where a PNR is identifiable and results in a failure, and the next possession by the same team is a PULL_UP field-goal attempt. A pilot run must estimate the expected count per team-season; if median < 25, the test is underpowered.
design.power: Assuming a true median lift of 2.5 pp (0.025 PPP) with SD ~0.15 PPP per unit, a one-sample t-test per unit at alpha=0.05 would require roughly 35-40 observations per unit for 80% power. Even 25 observations per unit would leave most units underpowered. The 70% threshold further reduces effective power. Formal power simulation needed.
design.controls: Shot distance, defender proximity (from tracking data if available), shot-clock remaining, period, score margin at start of possession, team fixed effects, season fixed effects. Baseline PPP estimated from team's pull-up shots in the same game state but not preceded by a PNR failure, using linear mixed models.
design.falsification: 1) Repeat the analysis for a placebo play type (e.g., CATCH_SHOOT) that should not be a counter; lift should be absent. 2) Repeat the analysis for pull-up after a successful PNR (score); the lift should be smaller or absent. 3) Check for regression-to-the-mean: compare PPP on the preceding PNR-fail possession with the team's overall PNR PPP; if the fail is unusually low, a subsequent lift may simply be mean reversion. 4) Use a pre-registered non-parametric bootstrap of team-season labels to assess chance of observing 70% positive under a global null.
design.multiplicity: Use Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control across all team-season units for the per-unit test of positive lift. Additionally, test the global hypothesis that median lift >2pp using a one-sample Wilcoxon test on the unit-level lifts.
design.decision_rule: Consider the hypothesis supported only if (a) at least 70% of team-season units show positive lift with FDR-adjusted one-sided p < 0.05, (b) the median lift across all units exceeds 0.02 PPP, and (c) all falsification checks pass at nominal alpha 0.05.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 per-game PBP and derived play-type possession records, with the post-rewrite play-type classifier that does not use assisted flags for unrealised outcomes.
